design_note: Expose how independent retry owners multiply backend attempts. The reader computes request amplification from constructed attempt caps instead of confusing one logical generation with one network operation.

source.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
source.concept: Retries at multiple layers can multiply downstream work during failures. Choosing an explicit retry owner limits this amplification.
source.scope: Original two-layer arithmetic uses constructed attempt caps and persistent retryable failures; it is not an AWS measurement or recommended configuration.

lesson.anchor: Failure modes and how to recognise them
lesson.title: Two retry owners can multiply one request
lesson.intro: ShopAssist requests one model response. Every network attempt fails with a retryable error. Compare four constructed configurations; each cap includes the first attempt, and the deadline permits every listed attempt.

data.rule: Worst-case attempts = application cap x adapter cap; successful earlier calls stop retrying.

read: Each application attempt starts a fresh adapter attempt allowance.
Both layers owning three attempts permits nine requests to the failing provider.
One retry owner keeps the total allowance explicit.
lesson.question: With the adapter capped at 3 attempts, what application cap reduces the worst case from 9 to 3?
lesson.answer: Set the application cap to 1, leaving transport retry ownership with the adapter. The bound becomes 1 x 3 = 3 network attempts for this logical request. A deadline can reduce attempts further; separate structured-output repairs still need their own accounting.
lesson.takeaway: Count retries across the whole call stack, not one loop at a time.
lesson.assumption: Constructed worst case: serial attempts, persistent retryable failures, no hidden retries and enough deadline. Counts are attempts, not extra retries.
